resolved_by: Supreme Court, United States v. Taylor, 596 U.S. 845 (2022), which held that attempted Hobbs Act robbery is not a crime of violence under § 924(c) because the attempt must itself involve actual, attempted, or threatened force.
issue: Is an attempt to commit an offense that qualifies as a crime of violence automatically a crime of violence under 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)?

sides.position: An attempt to commit a crime of violence is invariably a crime of violence, because § 924(c) reaches attempted use of force.
cases: United States v. Walker, 990 F.3d 316, 328 (3d Cir. 2021)
United States v. Smith, 957 F.3d 590, 595 (5th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Ingram, 947 F.3d 1021, 1026 (7th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Dominguez, 954 F.3d 1251, 1261 (9th Cir. 2020)
United States v. St. Hubert, 909 F.3d 335, 351 (11th Cir. 2018)

sides.position: An attempt is a crime of violence only if the attempt itself involves attempted, actual, or threatened force; an attempt to threaten force does not constitute an attempt to use force.
cases: United States v. Taylor, 979 F.3d 203, 209 (4th Cir. 2020), aff'd, 596 U.S. 845 (2022)
United States v. Hunt, 99 F.4th 161 (4th Cir. 2024)

this_court: The Fourth Circuit follows the rule it announced in Taylor, which the Supreme Court affirmed, so an attempt is a crime of violence only if the attempt itself involves attempted, actual, or threatened force.
quote: Our decision in Taylor created a split with our sister circuits, and the Supreme Court promptly took up the case.
cite: United States v. Martin Hunt, 99 F.4th 161 (4th Cir. 2024)
